section.title: May the Lord Answer in Trouble
section.sectionRationale: A royal psalm of communal intercession, likely sung by the people over their king before he went out to battle, pairing naturally with Psalm 21's thanksgiving after victory. It contrasts trust in chariots and horses with trust in the name of the LORD, a contrast that runs throughout Israel's history and anticipates the greater King whose victory did not come by military might.
section.thesis: The people's prayer for their king's success rests not on the strength of chariots or horses but entirely on the name of the LORD, a pattern of trust that finds its fullest expression in the victory of the greater King, Jesus Christ.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the congregation's prayer that the LORD would answer and support the king; their confident wish that his petitions be granted, followed by present tense confidence that the LORD saves His anointed; and the closing contrast between trust in chariots and horses versus trust in the name of the LORD.

units.label: May the Lord answer you
units.note: the people's prayer for the king

verses.text: May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you.
May He send you help from the sanctuary and sustain you from Zion.
May He remember all your gifts and look favorably on your burnt offerings. {{selah|Selah}}
May He give you the desires of your heart and make all your plans succeed.

units.label: Now I know the Lord saves His anointed

verses.text:
May we shout for joy at your victory and raise a banner in the name of our God. 
May the LORD grant all your petitions.

Now I know that the LORD saves His {{mashiach|anointed}}; He answers him from His holy heaven 
with the saving power of His right hand.

units.label: We trust in the name of the Lord
units.note: chariots and horses versus the name of the Lord

verses.text: Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.
They collapse and fall, but we rise up and stand firm.
O LORD, save the king. Answer us on the day we call.

selah.gloss: A musical or liturgical notation of uncertain precise meaning, likely indicating a pause, a rest, or a moment for reflection or instrumental interlude within the singing of the psalm.

mashiach.gloss: Anointed one, Messiah, one set apart for a God given office by anointing oil. Here applied to Israel's king, whose victories the people trace directly to God's saving power, a title and pattern of dependence later fulfilled completely in Jesus, the Messiah.

basic.context: This psalm captures the people of Israel praying together over their king before he goes out to battle, asking that the LORD would answer him, remember his offerings, and grant the desires of his heart. In the middle of the prayer, confidence rises, 'Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed'. The psalm closes with its most memorable line: some trust in chariots and horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God, a trust that alone leads to standing firm rather than collapsing.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm reflects the specific ancient practice of communal intercession for the king before battle, but its underlying principle, trusting God's name rather than human military strength, applies to every believer facing any kind of conflict or trial, not only kings facing armies.
basic.originalLanguages: The congregation prays for the king using selah, a pause for reflection, marking key moments in the prayer, and confidently names him God's mashiach, anointed one, whose victories come not from his own resources but from the saving power of God's right hand.
basic.typology: Israel's anointed king, dependent entirely on God rather than chariots or horses for victory, foreshadows Christ, the true and final Anointed One, whose decisive victory over sin and death came not through worldly power but through the seeming weakness of the cross.
basic.christ: The people's confidence that 'the LORD saves His anointed' anticipates, in its fullest sense, God's saving of Jesus Christ, His anointed Son, whose victory over death through resurrection came not by chariots or horses, worldly power, but by the greater power of God displayed through apparent weakness, 1 Corinthians 1:25.
basic.god: God is shown responding to communal, intercessory prayer for His anointed leader, and as the true source of any real victory, contrasted sharply with human military resources like chariots and horses that ultimately fail.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 21 is the natural companion thanksgiving psalm after this prayer's battle. Proverbs 21:31 states the horse is made ready for battle, but victory belongs to the LORD. Zechariah 4:6 declares victory comes not by might or power but by God's Spirit.
basic.oneStory: This communal prayer for Israel's king to be saved not by chariots or horses but by the name of the LORD anticipates the far greater pattern fulfilled in Christ, whose victory over sin and death came through the apparent weakness of the cross rather than worldly might, proving once again that salvation belongs to the LORD.

context.literary:
Psalm 20 is short and tightly made, and its shape is a conversation between voices. Verses 1 to 4 are a blessing spoken over the king in the second person, 'you' and 'your,' with four wishes: that God answer, help, remember and grant. Verses 5 to 8 turn on the phrase 'Now I know,' in verse 6, and move from the plural 'we' to the assured claim about the anointed and back to 'we' in verses 7 and 8. Verse 9 is a last cry that could have been shouted by the whole crowd.

Look at the way the words return. 'Answer' opens the psalm, verse 1, and closes it, verse 9, so that the first and last requests are the same. 'Name' appears in verse 1, 'name of the God of Jacob,' in verse 5, 'in the name of our God,' and in verse 7, 'the name of the LORD our God.' Salvation, the same root in 'victory' in verse 5 and 'saves' in verse 6 and 'save' in verse 9, wraps the whole. The psalm is built on four repeated words: answer, name, save, and the day, 'the day of trouble' in verse 1 and 'the day we call' in verse 9.

The psalm also has a hinge in the middle. The one word Selah after verse 3 marks a pause after the offerings are remembered, and what follows is the wish for the king's heart's desire. It is as if the sacrifice is offered in silence and then the prayer is spoken.

Psalm 20 is paired with Psalm 21. The people pray for the king before the battle, and the next psalm speaks of his joy in the salvation given, with echoes that link them: 'the desires of your heart,' Psalm 20:4, and 'You have granted his heart's desire,' Psalm 21:2. A request is answered in the next song.
context.historical:
Before Israel's kings went to war, sacrifice and prayer were the accepted way of seeking the LORD's help. Samuel offered a burnt offering and cried out to the LORD before the Philistines came near, and the LORD answered, 1 Samuel 7:9. Saul's fatal mistake was to offer the sacrifice himself, out of fear, rather than wait for Samuel, 1 Samuel 13:9-12. The psalm shows the right order: the offerings are remembered, the people pray, and the king waits for the answer from the sanctuary.

The setting is a liturgy of some kind at the sanctuary, where the king stands with a congregation who pray over him. The phrase 'from the sanctuary' and 'from Zion,' verse 2, places the help at the site of the LORD's dwelling, and the phrase 'from His holy heaven,' verse 6, places the answer at its source. The two locations belong together, since the sanctuary is where God's presence touches earth and heaven is where He rules.

Horses and chariots were the height of military technology, and they were the great fear of Israel when it met the peoples of Canaan and later Egypt and Aram. The law expected them to be a temptation: a king must not multiply horses for himself, Deuteronomy 17:16, and the same book tells Israel not to be afraid when they meet 'horses, chariots, and an army larger than yours,' Deuteronomy 20:1. David is remembered as a king who hamstrung captured chariot horses and kept only a hundred, 2 Samuel 8:4, whereas Solomon later gathered 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses, 1 Kings 10:26. The psalm's contrast is not between a modern and an ancient way of fighting but between two kinds of confidence that later kings would choose differently.

Isaiah looks back on that choice. Those who go down to Egypt for horses and chariots 'do not look to the Holy One of Israel,' Isaiah 31:1.
context.canonical:
The psalm's central contrast is one of the recurring themes of the Bible. In David's own life it appears in the fight with Goliath, when he says, 'I come against you in the name of the LORD of Hosts,' 1 Samuel 17:45, and that 'it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves,' 1 Samuel 17:47. Psalm 33:16-17 says that no king is saved by a great army and that 'A horse is a vain hope for salvation,' and Proverbs 21:31 says 'A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD.' Isaiah 31:1 and 30:16 warn against relying on horses, and the promise of Deuteronomy 20:1 stands behind them all.

The 'name' theme is equally deep. God revealed His name to Moses at the burning bush, Exodus 3:14-15, and told him that this was how He was to be remembered in every generation. Proverbs 18:10 says, 'The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run to it and are safe.' Psalm 20:1 prays that the name of the God of Jacob will protect the king, a title that recalls the God who answered Jacob 'in my day of distress,' Genesis 35:3, and Psalm 46:7 says that 'the God of Jacob is our fortress.'

The New Testament takes the words of verse 9 as the cry of Palm Sunday. The crowds shouted 'Hosanna,' from the same root as 'save,' 'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the King of Israel!' John 12:13, borrowing Psalm 118:25-26. The name of the LORD is now the name of Jesus, 'the name above all names,' Philippians 2:9, and 'there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved,' Acts 4:12.

At the end of the Bible the rider on the white horse, called Faithful and True, appears, Revelation 19:11, and the horses there are in His service and not in a rival's hands.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm meant to teach Israel how a nation goes to war, and the answer is that it goes to war by praying. The people are not spectators of the king's campaign; they are his intercessors. Every line of verses 1 to 5 is a wish spoken over the king by people who know that his success is their own, and the psalm gives the hearers the words to say. It is a psalm to be prayed by the congregation before it is a psalm to be admired.

It also means to move the hearers from anxiety to a settled confidence. The 'Now I know' of verse 6 is not a report about something that has already happened but a statement of faith that has become certain in the act of praying. The congregation is meant to leave the sanctuary knowing something they did not know when they came in.

And it means to show them where to place their trust. The final contrast, chariots and horses against the name of the LORD, is the lesson the whole psalm has been leading to. The point is not that horses are evil but that they cannot be the source of victory. A king and a people who remember that will still fight, but they will fight with their hands on the battle and their eyes on the LORD.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes an Israelite liturgy for a king going into battle. It does not command believers to expect victory in every conflict, nor does it promise that God will give whatever plan we make success, verse 4. The 'desires of your heart' are those of a king who is seeking God's purpose for his people, and the psalm's own sequence shows that the desires are shaped by the offerings and the name of the LORD, not the other way round.

What carries forward is the practice of praying for those in leadership, as Paul urges in 1 Timothy 2:1-2, and the deeper principle that God's people place their trust in Him and not in the tools they have. It does not forbid horses, insurance, medicine or strategy; it forbids resting our weight on them. Nor should the psalm be turned into a licence for war in God's name: the New Testament says the weapons of our warfare are not the world's, 2 Corinthians 10:4.

debates.question: Who is the speaker in verse 6, 'Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed', shifting from the plural 'we' of the earlier verses?

views.label: A priest or worship leader speaking a word of assurance to the king and congregation, perhaps after receiving a favorable sign or oracle
views.case: The shift from communal plea, verses 1-5, to confident personal declaration, verse 6, and back to plural in verses 7-9, suggests a liturgical structure where a priest or prophetic voice answers the congregation's prayer with assurance mid psalm.

views.label: The king himself speaking in the first person, expressing his own confidence in response to the people's intercession on his behalf
views.case: As the psalm's central figure and the one whose anointing, mashiach, is directly named, it is fitting for the king to voice his own settled trust at the psalm's turning point, responding to the people who have just prayed for him.

debates.bearing: Either reading preserves the psalm's essential structure and message, communal prayer met with confident assurance that God saves His anointed; the identity of the speaker in verse 6 does not change the psalm's central theological point about trusting God rather than human strength.

debates.question: How should verse 9 be divided: 'O LORD, save the king,' or 'Save, O LORD; may the King answer us'?

views.label: 'O LORD, save the king. Answer us on the day we call.'
views.case: This is the reading of the BSB text, and the Septuagint and Latin Vulgate read the line this way. It keeps the psalm's focus on the earthly king, which is where it began, and closes the circle: the prayer that opened with wishes for the king ends with the plain cry to save him.

views.label: 'Save, O LORD! May the King answer us on the day we call.'
views.case: The BSB footnote notes that the verb may also be read as 'give victory to,' and some readers follow the Hebrew accents in dividing the verse so that the King who answers is the LORD Himself. The psalm's word 'answer' in verse 1 and its closing 'answer' then have the same subject, the LORD, and the psalm ends by naming Him King.

debates.bearing: Either way, the psalm ends on the LORD's saving and answering. The second reading may add a note of God's kingship at the close, one that later readers, especially Christians, hear as pointing to the King who is both the anointed and the LORD.

debates.question: How do we hold together the prayer for the king's plans to succeed, verse 4, with the warning against trust in human strength, verse 7?

views.label: The plans are those God has already approved
views.case: The wish is placed after the request that God remember the offerings and receive the burnt sacrifice, verse 3. The plans that succeed are those of a king who is walking in worship and who is acting for the LORD's people, not those of self-reliance.

views.label: The petition is broad, and the psalm corrects it as it goes
views.case: On this reading the prayer of verse 4 is a general blessing that the psalm itself corrects by verse 7. What the people want is victory, but they find that what matters is the name of the LORD, so the desires of the heart are refocused in the act of praying.

debates.bearing: Both readings keep the psalm from promising that any project will succeed. What it does promise is that God answers those who look to Him, and it teaches the praying heart to want what He wants.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 begins with the verb anah, 'answer,' and the setting is 'the day of trouble,' yom tsarah, where tsarah comes from the root for 'narrow,' so trouble is a tight place. The same word is used by Jacob of the God who 'answered me in my day of distress,' Genesis 35:3, and the whole psalm can be heard as the blessing of the God of Jacob on a king in a tight place. In the same verse 'protect' is a form of the verb sagav, to be set high and out of reach, the root of misgav, the 'stronghold' of Psalm 18:2. To be protected is to be lifted beyond the enemy's reach.

Verse 2 asks God to 'sustain' the king, from saad, to support or hold up, as one steadies a person about to fall. Verse 3 asks God to 'remember' the offerings, from zakar. The word here is not a mental exercise: when God remembers, He acts. The reciprocal is in verse 7, where the Hebrew verb for what 'we' do with the name of the LORD is also a form of zakar, in a causative stem: we cause the name to be remembered, or we invoke it. The word 'trust' in the BSB and other versions is an interpretation. So God remembers the offerings of the king, and the people remember His name. The psalm is a chain of remembering.

'Look favorably on your burnt offerings' translates a verb related to deshen, fat or ashes, since the fat ashes of the sacrifice were what remained on the altar. The exact sense of the verb is debated, but the picture is of God accepting the offering as fully consumed on the altar. The burnt offering, olah, is 'that which goes up,' the sacrifice that rises to God entirely, Leviticus 1:3-4.

In verse 5 the word for 'raise a banner' is degel, the noun for the banners of the tribes in Numbers 2, and the verb is a form of the same word. The people plan to lift the flag in the name of their God as a public celebration of a victory that has not yet come.

Verse 6 begins with the words atta yadati, 'Now I know,' and the verb 'saves' is in the perfect tense. Hebrew can use the perfect for a certainty as good as done, so the sense is 'the LORD has saved,' or 'surely saves.' God's answer is 'from His holy heaven,' which balances the 'sanctuary' and 'Zion' of verse 2. The power is 'the saving power of His right hand,' gevurot yesha, the mighty acts of salvation.

In verse 8 'They collapse' is the verb kara, to kneel or bow, and the same root appears when David asks God to 'bring them to their knees' in Psalm 17:13. The people who trust in horses drop to their knees, while those who trust in the name 'rise up and stand firm,' a pair of verbs that pictures a standing up from a fall.

The last word of the psalm, in the BSB, is 'call,' from the verb qara, and in the Hebrew 'the day we call' matches 'the day of trouble' in the first line.

typology.type: The anointed king prayed over by his people, verses 1 to 6
typology.fulfillment: The people intercede for the mashiach as he goes out to fight. Jesus, the Anointed One, went out to the greatest battle not with the crowd's prayer but with His own, offering 'prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death,' and 'He was heard because of His reverence,' Hebrews 5:7. The desire of His heart, 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39, was granted in the resurrection. The type falls short because David's people prayed for him to win; Jesus' people were saved by His winning.

typology.type: Help from the sanctuary and from Zion, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: The help of the LORD came out of the sanctuary and Zion, where His presence met His people. In Christ the sanctuary is a person, 'the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and the help of God has come to earth in Him. The writer of Hebrews says believers approach 'Mount Zion, the city of the living God,' Hebrews 12:22. The type falls short because the help from Zion was for one nation and one king; in Christ it is offered to all who call on His name.

typology.type: Chariots and horses against the name of the LORD, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The contrast is given its supreme case at the cross. Christ won not by the strength of armies but through what looked like weakness, 'having disarmed the powers and authorities, He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross,' Colossians 2:15. He entered Jerusalem 'humble and riding on a donkey,' Zechariah 9:9, not on a warhorse. The type falls short because Israel's battles were fought with real swords under the psalm's prayer; the final victory is won by a suffering King, though at His return the rider on the white horse appears, Revelation 19:11.

The Hebrew of 'save' is the root behind 'Hosanna.' The crowd at the entry into Jerusalem cried out with the words of Psalm 118, John 12:13, and the cry of Psalm 20:9 is the same prayer that they were shouting at the King who had come. The Saviour was saving the world in the very hour they cried for a king to be saved. The type falls short because the psalm's king was saved from battle; the true King was not saved from the cross, so that His people might be.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by the word mashiach. The congregation says 'Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed,' and the Greek form of the word is Christos. Everything said in the psalm of the anointed king comes to rest on the One who is the Christ. The New Testament makes this claim in the prayer of the early church, when the believers quote Psalm 2 about the kings of the earth who take their stand 'against the Lord and against His Anointed One,' Acts 4:25-26. The anointed one of Psalm 20 is that King, and the people's prayer for the king before the battle has its perfect object in Him.

It leads to Christ by the pattern of the prayer that is answered. The wishes of verses 1 to 4 seem to be granted in Jesus' life in a way that no other king could have known. In the day of trouble He 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears,' Hebrews 5:7, and was heard. His offering was not a bull or a lamb but Himself, and God did more than 'look favorably' on it: He raised Him and set Him at His right hand, Ephesians 1:20. The psalm's 'saving power of His right hand,' verse 6, is the very power that raised Christ, since that hand is at work in the resurrection.

It leads to Christ by the contrast of chariots and the name. In a psalm about a king who does not trust horses, the King who is the fullest answer comes riding a donkey, Zechariah 9:9, and wins by the cross. Paul says the powers were 'disarmed' and put on public display, 'triumphing over them by the cross,' Colossians 2:15, a victory of an entirely different kind from the one the chariots promised. The name in which His people now stand is His own, and 'at the name of Jesus every knee should bow,' Philippians 2:10, an echo of the kneeling that overtakes the enemies in verse 8. He said, 'If you ask Me for anything in My name, I will do it,' John 14:14.

Finally, it leads to Christ by the cry of the crowd. On the road to Jerusalem they shouted 'Hosanna,' John 12:13, the cry of verse 9 in another form, and they meant it for a king. They did not understand that the King was riding to His death, and that His death was the answer to their prayer.

The caution is that Psalm 20 is not quoted in the New Testament as a prophecy of Christ. The links come from the word anointed, the theme of the name, and the shape of Jesus' victory, and are not from any single citation. It is also worth remembering that the psalm's prayer was answered for David in battle. Reading Christ into it does not remove that meaning but fills it out.
study.god:
The psalm gives us a God who answers. The first line and the last line of the psalm are the same request, and the words in between assume that a people who call will be heard. God in this psalm is not distant; He sends help from the sanctuary and sustains from Zion. The psalm's concept of prayer is that it is a real conversation with someone who responds.

He is the God of a name. The 'name of the God of Jacob,' verse 1, and 'the name of the LORD our God,' verse 7, are not magic words but stand for God's revealed character and presence, the God who spoke to Moses and who is known as the God of the patriarchs, Exodus 3:15. To trust in His name is to trust in who He has shown Himself to be. That gives the doctrine of God a personal side: He has made Himself known in a name that can be called on.

He is a God who remembers. The offerings are remembered, and the people remember Him. The picture is of a God whose attention is a gift and not an accident, who takes note of what is brought to Him, and who honours the worship of His people.

He is the God who saves by His own power. Verse 6 says He answers from 'His holy heaven' with the strength of His right hand. That combination of a heaven-based rule and a hand that reaches into a battle is the doctrine of providence. He is enthroned above all, and yet He acts on a particular day for a particular king. He does not need horses or chariots, and He is not against them; He simply is not dependent on them.

He is King. The psalm ends with the plea for the king, and on one reading it ends by naming God as the King who answers. The earthly king is real, but he is anointed, which means he serves under a higher rule. The psalm holds together the human king and the divine King without confusion.

For worship, the psalm gives the congregation words for praying over its leaders, and it gives every believer the chance to say what they are trusting. We are asked what our chariots and horses are, and taught to lift instead the name of the LORD, and to rise and stand firm.

crossReferences.note: Jacob speaks of God 'who answered me in my day of distress.' Psalm 20:1 prays that the LORD will answer in 'the day of trouble' and names Him the God of Jacob. The psalm gathers all of Israel's past experience of an answering God into a prayer for the king.

Samuel offers a burnt offering, cries out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answers, and the Philistines are routed. It is the pattern the psalm assumes: offerings remembered and a prayer heard before the battle is fought.

Saul, seeing his army scatter, offers the sacrifice himself instead of waiting. It is the opposite of Psalm 20, where the people wait and pray. It shows the danger of fear pushing a king to seize control when the LORD had asked him to trust.
When Israel sees 'horses, chariots, and an army larger than yours,' they are not to fear because the LORD who brought them from Egypt is with them. Psalm 20:7 is that command sung as a confession.

The companion psalm turns the wishes of Psalm 20 into thanks. 'You have granted his heart's desire' answers 'May He give you the desires of your heart,' and the king exults in the salvation the people asked for.

No king is saved by a great army and a horse is a vain hope for salvation. The psalm makes the same argument as Psalm 20:7, with the addition that the strength of the horse, however great, cannot save.

'A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD.' The proverb keeps the balance of Psalm 20. The horse is prepared, and the wise do not ignore preparation, but the outcome belongs to God.

David tells Goliath that he comes in the name of the LORD of Hosts. Psalm 20:7 is that same confidence in a congregation's voice, and it shows that David knew from experience what he was asking the people to pray.

Isaiah pronounces woe on those who go down to Egypt for help and trust in chariots and horsemen, and who do not look to the Holy One of Israel. It shows what happened when later kings chose the opposite of Psalm 20:7.

'The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run to it and are safe.' It uses the same root of being set on high as Psalm 20:1, 'protect,' and explains how a name can protect: it is the place a person runs to.

The crowd shouts 'Hosanna!' as Jesus enters Jerusalem. The word is from the root of 'save' in Psalm 20:9, and the shout of 'Blessed is the King of Israel' is a prayer for the salvation of the King who was coming to save.

Christ disarmed the powers and triumphed over them by the cross. It is the New Testament's answer to the contrast of Psalm 20:7, a victory not won by chariots but through a death, and it shows the psalm's principle at its deepest.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with people made to rule the earth under God, and it soon shows them trying to win security by their own devices. Cain builds a city, Babel builds a tower, and Egypt builds chariots. Against that background Psalm 20 is one of the clearest pictures of the alternative: a people who face real enemies and place their weight on the name of the LORD.

The psalm answers the question that runs through the books of Kings and the prophets, which is what makes a king safe. Israel is told in Deuteronomy that the king must not multiply horses, and the story shows kings who did, and who fell. David, who fought with a sling against a giant and hamstrung his captured horses, is the model that the psalm writes into liturgy. The exile is the end of the story of kings who trusted in their own strength.

The psalm also points forward. The anointed one who is saved by the LORD is the shape of a hope that outlasts the kings. Prophets speak of a King who comes 'humble and riding on a donkey,' Zechariah 9:9, and in Jesus that King arrives. His victory is won by the cross, and the crowd's cry of Hosanna is heard at last, not because the king is spared but because through Him God saves His people.

The church takes the psalm as its own. Believers are those who call on the name of the Lord, and they are promised salvation, Romans 10:13. They pray for their leaders and for one another, and they fight with weapons that are not the world's, 2 Corinthians 10:4. They also know what the psalm's people did not fully know, that the battle has been won.

In the new creation the horses and chariots are seen only in the service of the King who is called Faithful and True, Revelation 19:11, and the trust of God's people is no longer in anything that can fail. The name of the LORD is written on their foreheads, Revelation 22:4, and they stand firm forever.

quiz.q: What is the setting and purpose of this psalm?

options.text: A communal prayer of the people interceding for their king before he goes out to battle.
options.note: The psalm's language of trouble, sanctuary, offerings, and victory points to this specific pre-battle intercession.

options.text: A private prayer of thanksgiving after a personal healing.
options.note: The psalm is corporate in voice, 'we' and 'you', and concerns the king's battle, not a private healing.

options.text: A funeral lament for a fallen king.
options.note: The psalm looks forward to victory and answered prayer, not backward to mourning a death.

options.text: A wisdom instruction with no reference to the king.
options.note: The king is directly and repeatedly addressed throughout, making this a royal psalm, not general wisdom instruction.

quiz.q: What confident statement appears in verse 6?

options.text: 'Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed.'
options.note: This is the psalm's central turning point of rising confidence within the prayer.

options.text: 'The LORD has abandoned His anointed.'
options.note: This is the opposite of the psalm's actual declaration of confidence in God's salvation.

options.text: 'The king trusts only in his chariots.'
options.note: The psalm explicitly contrasts trust in chariots with trust in God's name, and the king's trust is placed in the LORD, not chariots.

options.text: 'No one can know whether the LORD will act.'
options.note: This directly contradicts the confident, settled tone of verse 6.

quiz.q: What contrast does the psalm draw in verse 7?

options.text: Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.
options.note: This is the psalm's most memorable and theologically central line.

options.text: Some trust in wealth, but we trust in wisdom.
options.note: The psalm's specific contrast is military resources, chariots and horses, versus trust in God's name, not wealth versus wisdom.

options.text: Some trust in prophets, but we trust in priests.
options.note: The contrast is between military might and trust in God, not between different human offices.

options.text: Some trust in the past, but we trust in the future.
options.note: This misses the psalm's specific and concrete contrast between military strength and trust in God's name.

quiz.q: What is the result of trusting chariots and horses versus trusting the LORD's name, according to verse 8?

options.text: Those who trust chariots and horses collapse and fall, but those who trust the LORD rise up and stand firm.
options.note: This vivid contrast shows the ultimate futility of human military strength apart from God.

options.text: Both groups experience identical outcomes regardless of where they place their trust.
options.note: The psalm draws a sharp distinction in outcomes, not an identical result for both groups.

options.text: Those who trust chariots gain lasting victory, while those who trust the LORD eventually fail.
options.note: This reverses the psalm's actual teaching, which favors trust in the LORD as leading to standing firm.

options.text: The psalm offers no comment on the outcome of either kind of trust.
options.note: Verse 8 explicitly states the outcome, collapse for one, standing firm for the other.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's pattern anticipate Christ?

options.text: It anticipates God saving His Anointed not through worldly military power but through what appeared to be weakness, as Christ's victory came through the cross.
options.note: The contrast between worldly strength and trust in God's name mirrors the pattern of God's power displayed through the apparent weakness of the crucifixion.

options.text: It predicts a specific future battle Jesus would fight with literal chariots.
options.note: The psalm's contrast is thematic and typological, not a literal prediction of Jesus using chariots in battle.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to the New Testament's teaching about Christ's victory.
options.note: The pattern of victory through apparent weakness rather than worldly strength connects clearly to New Testament teaching, such as 2 Corinthians 12:9-10.

options.text: It teaches that military strength is always sufficient for victory.
options.note: This is precisely the opposite of the psalm's teaching, which favors trust in God over military strength.

questions: This psalm shows a whole community praying together for their leader before a difficult challenge. Who in your life, a leader, a family member, a friend, could use this kind of intentional, corporate prayer support from you this week?

The people's confidence rises mid-prayer: 'Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed.' Have you experienced a moment where your own confidence in God grew stronger even while still in the middle of praying about something unresolved?

The psalm contrasts trusting chariots and horses with trusting the name of the LORD. What is your equivalent of 'chariots and horses', the resource, strategy, or strength you are tempted to trust in instead of God?

Verse 8 says those who trust human strength collapse, while those who trust the LORD stand firm. Where in your life right now do you need to consciously shift your trust from your own resources to God's name?
Christ's decisive victory came through the apparent weakness of the cross, not worldly power. How does this reshape the way you think about strength and weakness in your own circumstances?

translationNotes.note: Selah likely marks a pause for musical interlude or reflection; its precise musical function remains uncertain, though it consistently highlights significant moments in a psalm.
Anointed renders mashiach, applied here to Israel's king, the same title, Messiah, later given in its fullest sense to Jesus Christ.

Chariots and horses represent the height of ancient military technology; the psalm's contrast with trusting the LORD's name would have been immediately understood as a comparison between worldly power and covenant faith.
